title: Query Data (SELECT)
structure:
SELECT column1, column2
FROM table_name
[WHERE condition]
[ORDER BY column_name];
example:
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name
FROM customer
ORDER BY customer_id
LIMIT 10;
output:
customer_id | first_name | last_name
-------------+------------+-----------
           1 | MARY       | SMITH
           2 | PATRICIA   | JOHNSON
           3 | LINDA      | WILLIAMS
...
note: Name columns explicitly. SELECT * silently changes result shape when schemas change and can fetch expensive or sensitive fields.

title: DDL Commands
output:
CREATE TABLE
ALTER TABLE
DROP TABLE
note: DDL can take locks and block applications. Review lock behavior and make destructive migrations reversible.

title: DML Commands
note: Run the same WHERE clause as SELECT first and check its count. Use a transaction for multi-step changes.

title: Filtering Data
structure:
SELECT column_list
FROM table_name
WHERE condition1 [AND | OR condition2]
ORDER BY column_name;
example:
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, active
FROM customer
WHERE active = 1 AND first_name ILIKE 'A%' AND customer_id BETWEEN 1 AND 100
ORDER BY last_name;
output:
customer_id | first_name | last_name | active
-------------+------------+-----------+--------
          53 | ANDREA     | HENDERSON |      1
          80 | ANGELA     | HERNANDEZ |      1
...
note: A leading wildcard, such as ILIKE '%term', usually defeats a normal B-tree index. Measure and use a suitable search index when needed.

title: SQL Joins (Basics)
example:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, a.address FROM customer AS c INNER JOIN address AS a ON a.address_id = c.address_id;
SELECT c.customer_id, r.rental_id FROM customer AS c LEFT JOIN rental AS r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id;
note: Keep relationship predicates in ON. A right-table filter in WHERE can inadvertently turn a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

title: SQL Joins (Advanced)
example:
SELECT f.title, cat.name AS category FROM film AS f JOIN film_category AS fc ON fc.film_id = f.film_id JOIN category AS cat ON cat.category_id = fc.category_id;
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customer AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM rental AS r WHERE r.customer_id = c.customer_id);
output:
title       | category
------------------+----------
 ACADEMY DINOSAUR | Documentary
 ACE GOLDFINGER   | Horror
...

 customer_id
-------------
           1
...
note: Many-to-many joins multiply rows. Establish the intended grain before aggregating; DISTINCT can hide, not repair, a bad join.

title: Set Operators
note: UNION removes duplicates and may need a costly de-duplication step. Use UNION ALL unless set semantics are required.

title: SQL Functions
structure:
SELECT function_name(column1) AS derived_value
FROM table_name;
note: A function applied to a filtered column can prevent an ordinary index from being used. Verify the plan before optimizing.

title: String Functions
structure:
SELECT CONCAT(column1, ' ', column2) AS combined_text, UPPER(column1) AS upper_text
FROM table_name;
output:
customer_id | full_name        | last_name_upper | email_prefix
-------------+------------------+-----------------+-------------
           1 | MARY SMITH       | SMITH           | MARY.
           2 | PATRICIA JOHNSON | JOHNSON         | PATRI
...
note: CONCAT and the concatenation operator can handle NULL differently. Decide whether a missing value should be empty or remain unknown.

title: Numeric Functions
structure:
SELECT numeric_column, ROUND(expression, decimal_places) AS rounded_value
FROM table_name;
note: Use fixed-precision decimal types for money, not floating point. Define rounding at the business boundary.

title: Date and Time Functions
example:
SELECT rental_id, rental_date, return_date, rental_date::date AS rental_day, date_trunc('month', rental_date) AS rental_month, return_date - rental_date AS rental_duration
FROM rental
WHERE rental_date >= date '2005-06-01'
LIMIT 10;
note: Use half-open timestamp ranges (>= start AND < next_start) to preserve index use and avoid end-of-day precision bugs.

title: NULL Functions
structure:
SELECT COALESCE(column_name, fallback_value) AS value, NULLIF(value1, value2) AS nullable_value
FROM table_name;
note: COALESCE can mask data-quality issues. Preserve raw NULLs in analytical layers unless a business default is defined.

title: Case Statement
structure:
SELECT CASE WHEN condition1 THEN result1 WHEN condition2 THEN result2 ELSE fallback_result END AS label
FROM table_name;
note: CASE stops at the first match. Order overlapping conditions from most specific to least specific and test boundaries.

title: Aggregate Functions
structure:
SELECT group_column, COUNT(*) AS row_count, SUM(numeric_column) AS total_value
FROM table_name
[WHERE row_condition]
GROUP BY group_column
[HAVING aggregate_condition];
example:
SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS payment_count, sum(amount) AS total_paid, avg(amount) AS average_payment
FROM payment
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING sum(amount) >= 100
ORDER BY total_paid DESC;
note: WHERE filters source rows; HAVING filters aggregated groups. Do not use HAVING for row-level conditions.

title: Window Functions Basics
structure:
SELECT columns, aggregate_function(value) OVER (PARTITION BY group_column) AS window_value
FROM table_name;
note: Window functions keep the original row count. Large partitions can require costly sorting and memory.

title: Window Aggregate
structure:
SELECT columns, SUM(value) OVER (PARTITION BY group_column ORDER BY sort_column ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM table_name;
note: Specify ROWS explicitly. The default frame can treat equal ORDER BY values as peers rather than incremental rows.

title: Window Ranking
structure:
SELECT columns, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_column ORDER BY sort_column DESC) AS row_number
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT customer_id, payment_id, amount, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS row_num, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS payment_rank, dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS dense_payment_rank
FROM payment;
note: Add a stable tie-breaker when order matters. Without one, ROW_NUMBER can vary between executions.

title: Window Value
structure:
SELECT columns, LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY group_column ORDER BY sort_column) AS previous_value, LEAD(value) OVER (PARTITION BY group_column ORDER BY sort_column) AS next_value
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT customer_id, payment_date, amount, lag(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id) AS previous_amount, lead(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id) AS next_amount, first_value(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id) AS first_amount
FROM payment;
note: FIRST_VALUE observes the current frame. Set an explicit frame when you need a value across the full partition.

title: Subqueries
structure: SELECT column_list FROM outer_table WHERE column_name IN (SELECT column_name FROM inner_table WHERE condition);
example: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name FROM customer WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM payment GROUP BY customer_id HAVING sum(amount) >= 100);
output:
customer_id | first_name | last_name
-------------+------------+----------
         148 | ELEANOR    | HUNT
         178 | MARION     | SNYDER
...
note: For existence checks, EXISTS avoids NULL-related surprises from NOT IN. Compare plans rather than assuming one form always wins.

title: Common Table Expressions (CTE)
structure:
WITH result_name AS (SELECT columns FROM table_name WHERE condition)
SELECT columns FROM result_name;
example: WITH customer_spend AS (SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) AS total_paid FROM payment GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, cs.total_paid FROM customer AS c JOIN customer_spend AS cs ON cs.customer_id = c.customer_id ORDER BY cs.total_paid DESC;
note: CTEs improve readability but are not automatically faster. Engines differ on whether they materialize or inline them.

title: Views
output:
CREATE VIEW
 customer_id | payment_count | total_paid
-------------+---------------+-----------
         148 |            45 |    211.55
...
DROP VIEW
note: A standard view stores its query, not its result. Treat it as an API and keep its columns and semantics stable.

title: CTAS and Temp Tables
structure:
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE temp_table AS SELECT columns FROM source_table WHERE condition;
SELECT aggregate_function(column_name) FROM temp_table;
example:
CREATE TEMP TABLE recent_rentals AS SELECT rental_id, customer_id, rental_date FROM rental WHERE rental_date >= date '2005-07-01';
SELECT count(*) FROM recent_rentals;
note: Temporary tables are session-scoped but still consume resources. Index large temporary datasets used in repeated joins.

title: Stored Procedures
structure:
CREATE PROCEDURE procedure_name(parameter_name data_type) BEGIN -- statements END;
CALL procedure_name(argument_value);
note: Document procedure side effects and transaction behavior; this differs by database and calling context.

title: Triggers
structure: CREATE TRIGGER trigger_name BEFORE | AFTER INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE ON table_name FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE trigger_function;
output:
CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE TRIGGER
DROP TRIGGER
DROP FUNCTION
note: Triggers make writes implicit and may amplify bulk work. Keep them minimal and document their side effects.

title: Indexes
output:
CREATE INDEX
 payment_id | amount
------------+-------
      16017 |  5.99
      16018 |  0.99
...
DROP INDEX
note: Every index costs storage and writes. Design composite indexes from real predicates and verify actual use with the planner.

title: Execution Plan
structure: EXPLAIN [ANALYZE] [options] SELECT columns FROM table_name WHERE condition;
example: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT c.customer_id, sum(p.amount) AS total_paid FROM customer AS c JOIN payment AS p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE p.payment_date >= timestamp '2005-06-01' GROUP BY c.customer_id;
output:
HashAggregate  (cost=... rows=... width=...) (actual time=... rows=599 loops=1)
   Group Key: c.customer_id
   ->  Hash Join  (cost=... rows=... width=...)
         Hash Cond: (p.customer_id = c.customer_id)
...
note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. Do not point it at an unbounded mutation in production.

title: Partitions
structure:
CREATE TABLE parent_table (columns) PARTITION BY RANGE (partition_key);
CREATE TABLE child_table PARTITION OF parent_table FOR VALUES FROM (start_value) TO (end_value);
note: Partitioning needs a retention, indexing, and partition-creation strategy. Pruning only works when predicates align with the partition key.
